strengths: Novel and well-motivated benchmark: FingerTip 20K is the first mobile GUI benchmark to evaluate proactive task suggestion and personalized task execution, addressing a genuine gap in existing datasets that are passive and instruction-driven (clearly contrasted in Table 1).

Distinctive data collection methodology: collecting 21,437 episodes from 95 real users on their own devices over a month, with contextual information (time, location, user profile) and longitudinal usage patterns, yields data that is qualitatively different from simulator-based datasets like AitW or AndroidControl.

Comprehensive and layered evaluation: experiments cover generalist MLLMs, prompt-engineered agents, and specialized GUI-control models; fine-tuning experiments with LoRA rank/data-size sweeps; difficulty analysis; human baseline; and extensive appendix experiments (OOD generalization on unseen users/apps/intents, contextual-info ablations, probability-distribution setting, Sim2 validity via user study, cheating check for identical tasks).
Honest treatment of ethics and limitations: privacy screening during data collection, informed consent, explicit discussion of re-identification risks, regional bias, and broader impacts.

Empirically demonstrates the problem is real and hard: all models perform far below the human baseline (12.8% vs 30.3% SR1), and fine-tuning on the collected data yields substantial, coherent gains across tracks.
weaknesses: Limited generalizability: all 95 users are from mainland China and interact almost exclusively with Chinese apps; linguistic habits, UI layouts, and action patterns may not transfer, which weakens the claimed universality of the benchmark despite the authors' acknowledgment.

Metric soundness concerns: SR1 depends on DeepSeek-V3 as an LLM judge without validation against human judgments or inter-annotator agreement; Sim1 is an ad-hoc average of cosine and Levenshtein similarity; Sim2 (Levenshtein ratio over raw action strings) is a crude proxy for 'personalization' that can be gamed or may not reflect meaningful preference alignment (the user study in Table 13 helps but is limited to 200 episodes and 4 models).

The proactive task suggestion task may be inherently underdetermined: user intents at a given moment are stochastic, and even humans achieve only 30.3% SR1; the paper does not report how well different humans agree, making it unclear whether low model scores reflect capability limits or irreducible task ambiguity.

Potential memorization/leakage in the fine-tuning results: fine-tuning and test data come from the same 95 users (test set is the last 20% by time), so improved performance could partly reflect user-specific memorization rather than learned generalization; the OOD analysis partially addresses this but on very small subsets (99-126 episodes).

Evaluation infrastructure limitations: SR2 is determined by manual checking; the environment is a physical USB-connected phone, limiting reproducibility as a standardized testbed; the execution test set contains only 200 episodes, so differences of a few percentage points have wide uncertainty (no confidence intervals or significance tests anywhere in the paper).

Fine-tuning experiments are narrow (single 7B model, LoRA only), and the paper does not compare fine-tuning against strong alternatives such as retrieval-based in-context personalization at scale, leaving open whether the benchmark's gains require fine-tuning.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely underexplored problem: proactively suggesting tasks and personalizing execution for mobile GUI agents, moving beyond the standard passive 'follow-the-instruction' setting of existing benchmarks (AitW, AndroidControl, AMEX, etc.).

The data collection effort is substantial and distinctive: 21,437 episodes from 95 users collected longitudinally (~1 month) on their own physical phones in real daily usage, with contextual metadata (time, location category, user profile) and historical intent/action linkage that no prior mobile GUI dataset provides.

A broad evaluation is performed across generalist MLLMs (GPT-4.1, Qwen variants, DeepSeek-VL2), prompt-engineered agents (AutoDroid, AppAgent), and specialized GUI-control models (UI-TARS, CogAgent, Aguvis), plus fine-tuning experiments with LoRA and supplementary analyses (out-of-domain subsets, joint vs. separate fine-tuning, context ablations, cold-start, probability-distribution setting, Sim2 validity study).

The paper includes a human study (30.3% vs. 12.8% best model), attempts to validate the personalization metric against user ratings (Table 13), and addresses cheating concerns for in-context action references (Table 14). Ethics, limitations, and broader impact sections are present and reasonably candid.
weaknesses: The validity of the core evaluation metrics is questionable. SR1 for proactive suggestion is decided by DeepSeek-V3 as an LLM judge with no reported human agreement analysis, and Sim1 (average of embedding cosine and Levenshtein similarity) is a crude proxy for intent equivalence. The Sim2 metric for personalization (ratio of Levenshtein similarity to the target user vs. a different-type user) is ad hoc, sensitive to action-sequence tokenization, and its correlation with subjective preference is only weakly supported by a small study (4 models, 200 episodes).

The proactive task suggestion track appears close to ill-posed: even humans only reach 30.3% success, and best models ~12.8%, with the main gains seemingly coming from memorizing individual users' habitual intents (time- and scenario-conditioned). It is unclear the benchmark measures genuine 'proactivity' rather than per-user pattern memorization, especially since training and test data share the same users; the user-unseen analysis in the appendix only covers 3 users / 126 episodes.

Evaluation sets are small and partially problematic: the personalized execution test set has only 200 episodes, success is judged manually (subjective, no inter-annotator agreement reported), the 2.5x golden-step failure threshold is arbitrary, and the two test sets contain overlapping episodes.

The Fig. 5 'personalized action analysis' that motivates the personalization track is statistically weak: it samples only ONE episode per intent category per comparison, yet draws conclusions about measurable user-preference differences.

Generalizability is limited: all data comes from 95 users in mainland China using Chinese apps, in Chinese language; the paper acknowledges this but it substantially constrains the impact of the benchmark as a community resource.

Several evaluation design choices may disadvantage baselines: a single simple prompt is used for all generalist models on the new track, and specialized agents' original prompts are retrofitted with new inputs; no sensitivity analysis over prompting is provided. Also, only a single 7B model (Qwen-2.5-VL-7B) is fine-tuned with LoRA, limiting the strength of the fine-tuning conclusions.
Reproducibility is undermined by missing/broken links in the submission (the open-source URL and data-release URL are blank in the text), which prevents verification of code and data claims.

The setting of zero input screenshots for headline results is somewhat artificial for a deployed 'proactive' assistant, and Table 10 shows performance depends heavily on inputs (13.8% with 3 screenshots + full history), suggesting headline numbers reflect the hardest, least realistic configuration rather than a practical operating point.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated benchmark: FingerTip 20K is, to my knowledge, the first mobile GUI agent benchmark targeting proactive task suggestion and personalized task execution, filling a genuine gap identified in the related-work comparison (Table 1).

High-quality data collection methodology: demonstrations are gathered from 95 users on their own physical devices during real daily usage over a month, rather than simulators with author-defined instructions, yielding longitudinal, context-enriched data (21,437 episodes, 506 apps) that plausibly reflects real user intents and habits.

Comprehensive evaluation: the paper tests both generalist MLLMs (GPT-4.1, Qwen family, DeepSeek-VL2) and GUI-specific agents (UI-TARS, CogAgent, Aguvis, AppAgent, AutoDroid), reports a human baseline showing a large model-human gap, and includes fine-tuning experiments demonstrating the data's utility.

Unusually thorough appendix: OOD generalization tests (user/app/intent-unseen), track-interaction analysis, ablations on contextual information and history, a probability-distribution variant of suggestion, a user study validating Sim2 against subjective ratings, and a check for cheating via identical task retrieval — these proactively address many anticipated reviewer concerns.
The personalized action analysis (Figure 5) provides empirical evidence that user-specific action preferences exist and are measurable, grounding the motivation for the personalized execution track.

Ethics and privacy considerations are discussed substantively (screening for private content, consent, broader impacts including risks of longitudinal screen capture), with limitations honestly acknowledged.
weaknesses: Limited generalizability: all 95 users are in mainland China and the apps are almost exclusively Chinese (WeChat, Rednote, Bilibili, etc.), so intents, UI layouts, and action patterns may not transfer; this significantly narrows the benchmark's claimed scope, though the authors acknowledge it.

Small and subjective evaluation for personalized execution: the execution test set contains only 200 episodes, and success (SR2) is judged by manual inspection — presumably by the authors — without reported inter-annotator agreement or blinding; this raises reliability concerns for the headline numbers.

The Sim2 personalization metric is crude: Levenshtein similarity over action-sequence strings is a fragile proxy for 'preference', values above 1.0 are semantically awkward, and although the user study (Table 13) shows positive correlation, it covers only four models on 200 episodes and the correlation appears weak for some pairs (e.g., GPT-4.1 vs Qwen-7B orderings).

Proactive suggestion may be partially ill-posed: intent prediction with zero screenshots is a high-entropy task, so low model scores (max 12.8%) may reflect inherent ambiguity of the task rather than a fixable model deficiency; the human baseline of 30.3% on only a 400-episode subset also suggests the task is hard even for humans, complicating interpretation of the 'gap'.
Reliance on LLM-as-judge (DeepSeek-V3) for the binary SR1 success criterion without reported human verification of the judge's accuracy.

Fine-tuning evidence is narrow: only Qwen-2.5-VL-7B with LoRA, and fine-tuned models still trail UI-TARS substantially in execution success (15.5% vs 38.5%), so the claim of 'excellent performance' from fine-tuning should be tempered; cost constraints limited larger-scale experiments.

Data collection protocol introduces potential biases: the daily cap of 12 uploads, reminder prompts, and training-phase guidance may skew intent distribution; self-selected crowdworkers recording their own intents also invite selection effects not analyzed in the paper.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the manuscript: the data release and anonymous code links are left blank ('released at .'), so at review time neither the data nor the evaluation pipeline can be verified.
